newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-EU move on chip imports satisfies no-one.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU move on chip imports satisfies no-one.

text.p: The European Commission's decision to introduce minimum prices on certain imports of computer chips has caught all sides of the industry unawares -- and nobody seems to be happy.

European manufacturers of dynamic random access memory (D-RAM) chips say the move does not go far enough to protect the fragile market, computer makers are angered that now they cannot buy the cheapest available, and consumers will pay for the affair at shops throughout the EU.
"It is a classic no-win situation," said a European Commission official. "You could see this one coming from a long way off."
But Eckhart Runge, secretary-general of the European Electronic Component Manufacturers Association, told Reuters the Commission's move was unexpected and did not go far enough.
Although reluctant to comment until he had had more time to discuss the issue with chip makers, Runge said: "It caught everyone by surprise.
"We had requested as long ago as June last year for the Commission to reintroduce anti-dumping measures after we had provided them with evidence of dumping and injury to European manufacturers."

The Commission said on Monday it was introducing minimum prices on D-RAM computer chips originating in Japan and South Korea with immediate effect, although in reality prices will rise only next month.
The EU imposed anti-dumping duties on Japanese exporters in January 1990 and later on South Korean exporters, but the measures were suspended 21 months ago because D-RAM prices were rising.
But there is now a glut of D-RAM chips -- used in products ranging from mobile telephones to computers -- and the EU has decided to re-introduce protection measures.

The move follows complaints from European chip producers who have accused their South Korean and Japanese counterparts of selling chips products at below manufacturing cost in Europe in order to protect market share.

Officials would not say what the new minimum prices would be although they said they had told the relevant companies -- an approach they said was to preserve the commercial confidentiality of information supplied to the Commission inquiry.

The EU market for D-RAM chips was worth five billion European currency units ($5.7 billion) in 1995, a Commission official said, of which South Korean and Japanese manufactureres have over 60 percent.
Measures are intended to protect EU producers of D-RAMs which include Motorola, Siemens and Texas Instruments, the official said.
The Commission spokesman said 12 Japanese and three South Korean companies were involved but he declined to give any names.

An official from a European electronics manufacturing association -- who declined to be identified until the EU move had been studied more closely -- said his organisation regretted any move that did not allow them the opportunity to buy from the cheapest source.
"It is inevitable that any price rise in components will have to be passed on to consumers," he said. "The stupid thing is that for us, it is a price rise that simply does not need to happen."
